articles.title: Understory diversity is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration
articles.titleEn: Understory diversity is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration
articles.abstract: Forests are a major terrestrial carbon sink, and higher overstory diversity is often associated with greater carbon accrual in trees and soils. Yet the contribution of the understory vegetation, the most species-rich forest stratum, to tree and soil carbon accumulation remains largely unknown. Here, we analyzed Canada’s National Forest Inventory database to explore whether understory diversity (richness and evenness of shrubs, herbs, and bryophytes) is associated with carbon accumulation in overstory trees and soils across environmental gradients of air temperature, climate moisture, and nitrogen deposition. We found that herb and bryophyte species richness were positively associated with decadal tree carbon accumulation, with the strongest effects at warmer, drier, and nitrogen-limited sites. In contrast, understory diversity showed no consistent association with soil carbon accumulation. On a decadal scale, increasing herb and bryophyte species richness from their minimum to median values corresponded to 15% and 6% increases in tree carbon accumulation, respectively. These results provide large-scale observational evidence that diversity in lower vegetation layers is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration and reveal strong environmental modulation of these multistratal biodiversity–ecosystem functioning relationships. These findings suggest that species-rich herb and bryophyte communities should be considered in strategies for sustaining forest carbon sinks, especially under warmer, drier conditions and nutrient limitation.

articles.title: Geography of groundwater use and depletion in internationally shared aquifers
articles.titleEn: Geography of groundwater use and depletion in internationally shared aquifers
articles.abstract: Transboundary aquifers (TBAs) underlie 35% of global groundwater-irrigated cropland, yet few are covered by formal cooperative arrangements. Whether this limited cooperation is consequential depends in part on where groundwater is used within shared aquifers, because pumping far from international borders may generate little cross-border impact. Combining ∼ 116,000 well observations with global irrigation data across all 426 known TBAs, we assess how groundwater use and depletion differ from comparable domestic systems and how they are distributed relative to international borders. While we find no evidence of greater average depletion in TBAs, depletion is more strongly concentrated toward international borders in shared aquifers and varies substantially across systems. Irrigation is also more intensive and concentrated toward borders in shared aquifers, although much of this pattern is attenuated after accounting for border rivers. Groundwater-supplied irrigation remains more border-proximate after accounting for these rivers. A dyad-level typology distinguishes shared systems according to where groundwater demand is concentrated, linking their potential for cross-border interaction to different management options. These findings suggest that transboundary groundwater governance should be organized around the geography of groundwater use and potential cross-border interactions rather than treating shared aquifers as uniform governance units.

articles.title: Modeling the global potential of smart farming innovations
articles.titleEn: Modeling the global potential of smart farming innovations
articles.abstract: Smart farming innovations can improve agricultural productivity, resilience, and environmental sustainability, yet their real-world impact hinges on their diffusion dynamics, which in turn depend on their economic viability. We present here a global assessment of the profitability of smart farming innovation across croplands at a spatial resolution of ~5 km from the farmers’ and the societal perspectives. We cover application mapping for precision agriculture, automated application of inputs, autonomous weeding machines, GPS steering assistance systems, and autonomous irrigation systems. For this, we compiled a globally comprehensive dataset of smart farming innovation adoption locations (N = 4,422) based on a combination of a survey (N = 2,677) and a meta-analysis (N = 1,745) and combined them with remotely sensed and statistical data to train an ensemble of five geospatial machine learning models (generalized linear models, random forests, support vector machines, maximum entropy, and boosted regression trees), which show the global distribution of the different innovations’ profitability and its overlap with major environmental issues the innovations can help to mitigate. Simulations of future socioeconomic pathways combined with assumptions about future agri-environmental policies reveal that, especially in middle-income countries, the potential of smart farming will grow over time.

articles.title: Immense but not immutable: A sudden and sustained decline in deep-pelagic life in a large oceanic ecosystem
articles.titleEn: Immense but not immutable: A sudden and sustained decline in deep-pelagic life in a large oceanic ecosystem
articles.abstract: The deep-pelagic habitat of the Gulf of Mexico comprises 90.4% of its volume and houses an exceptionally diverse deep-pelagic animal community that provides numerous ecosystem services, including carbon cycling and prey provisioning for oceanic predators. Here, we report sudden, severe, and persistent declines in the abundance of deep-pelagic fishes, crustaceans, and cephalopods that have persisted for over a decade. Over a 3.5-y period, animal abundances declined by 60 to 85%, taxon depending. Particularly hard-hit were ecologically foundational taxa such as euphausiids and lanternfishes. The magnitude of population-level decline that occurred during this 3.5-y period was greater than any observed over a 60-y period in the California Current system, the only comparable dataset, making this the fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type. These declines were detected both via direct sampling and acoustic sensing, providing independent corroboration. Genomic analyses indicate reductions in genetic diversity among dominant taxa, both a corroboration and a consequence of the decline. Furthermore, resource managers report that these trends parallel those of managed or protected Gulf species that are dependent on deep-pelagic prey, including endangered species (e.g., beaked whales, Rice’s whale). No naturally occurring factors (e.g., temperature, oxygen, food supply) correlated with the observed declines, suggesting an anthropogenic proximate cause. That the declines began shortly after the Deepwater Horizon oil spill points to that event as the most parsimonious explanation. These findings suggest that despite its immense size the deep-pelagic biome is vulnerable to human-induced disturbance and possesses limited resilience to facilitate recovery.

articles.title: A Bering Sea marine heatwave triggers unprecedented crab hybridization, challenging fisheries management
articles.titleEn: A Bering Sea marine heatwave triggers unprecedented crab hybridization, challenging fisheries management
articles.abstract: Marine heatwaves are increasingly recognized for their capacity to generate ecological surprises, yet the pathways that propagate these unexpected responses are often poorly understood. Here, we document an unanticipated ecological response 7 y after a Bering Sea marine heatwave, in which formerly rare snow crab ( Chionoecetes opilio ) × Tanner crab ( C. bairdi ) hybrid abundance increased 13.4-fold, and the proportion of commercial-sized hybrid males increased 13.1-fold, relative to historical averages. Using causal modeling, we show that the hybrid crab surge was mediated by a heatwave-induced collapse of snow crab rather than direct thermal effects on hybrid survival or increased spatial overlap between mature snow and Tanner crab. Our results reveal an indirect cascading pathway through which an extreme climate event triggered unexpected ecological consequences and unforeseen challenges for fisheries management in the Bering Sea. The dramatic increase in abundance of harvestable hybrid crab, coupled with their exclusion from existing management frameworks, highlights the vulnerability of inflexible management systems to unanticipated ecosystem responses.

articles.title: Toward cooler cities by larger homogeneous functional clusters
articles.titleEn: Toward cooler cities by larger homogeneous functional clusters
articles.abstract: Urban heat island (UHI) intensifies heat-related risks and environmental degradation in cities worldwide, yet existing mitigation strategies have largely overlooked how the spatial scale of homogeneous functional building clusters influences local climate. This scale may matter because buildings with similar functions often share similar morphology, activity schedules, and anthropogenic heat-release patterns, allowing their spatial contiguity to shape ventilation and heat accumulation. Here, we introduce the Urban Homogeneous Scale (UHS)—an indicator that measures the spatial scale of contiguous, functionally similar building clusters—and analyze 233,844 observations across 101 global cities to assess its potential for mitigating surface UHI. We find that larger UHS is associated with lower surface UHI: every 100-meter increase in UHS corresponds to 4.5% decrease in daytime UHI. This daytime cooling effect is particularly more pronounced in inland, humid, and high-income regions. In low-income regions, larger building area and higher building volume more strongly weaken UHS cooling capacity than in wealthier regions, revealing a socioeconomic inequality in UHS’s mitigation benefits. Our findings identify the spatial scale of building clusters as a essential dimension of urban form associated with urban heat burden, and suggest that considering UHS alongside targeted controls on built environmental characteristics may inform future heat-mitigation planning.

articles.title: mechanoLight: A genetically encoded fluorescent biosensor for visualizing 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction in live cells
articles.titleEn: mechanoLight: A genetically encoded fluorescent biosensor for visualizing 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction in live cells
articles.abstract: G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs) are pivotal sensors of the mechanical environment, yet how they sense and transduce physical stimuli into biochemical signals within live cells remains largely elusive. Here we introduce mechanoLight, a genetically encoded red fluorescent biosensor designed to report the mechanical activation of the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A receptor (5-HT2AR). By incorporating a circularly permuted mApple (cp-mApple) into the third intracellular loop of 5-HT2AR with the optimized linker (m-linker), mechanoLight selectively detects conformational changes of 5-HT2AR in response to fluid shear stress while exhibiting minimal sensitivity to 5-HT. In sharp contrast, psychLight2, the previously developed green 5-HT2AR biosensor, primarily detects ligand-induced 5-HT2AR activation, suggesting that mechanoLight and psychLight2 capture distinct conformational modes of 5-HT2AR activation. Integrated analysis of linker-swapping experiments, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the flexibility of the m-linker underlies the mechanosensitivity of mechanoLight. We further extend this strategy to other mechanosensitive GPCRs, enabling visualization of their mechanoreactivity in live cells. The mechanoLight signal reflects the mechanosensitivity of 5-HT2AR, as shear stress-induced 5-HT2AR activation triggers Gα q -dependent signaling pathways, including phospholipase C (PLC) activation, intracellular Ca 2+ mobilization, and ERK phosphorylation. Mutational analysis further identifies N-terminal glycosylation and helix 8 as structural determinants of 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction. Together, our findings establish 5-HT2AR as a mechanotransducer and introduce mechanoLight as a powerful tool for deciphering the molecular principles of GPCR mechanotransduction in live cells.

articles.title: Leveraging existing grid infrastructure for rapid US renewable and storage deployment
articles.titleEn: Leveraging existing grid infrastructure for rapid US renewable and storage deployment
articles.abstract: Rapid electricity demand growth, grid connection delays, and supply chain constraints create a serious risk of supply shortages and rising electricity costs in the next few years. This paper studies the strategy of adding colocated renewables and storage at existing power plants to take advantage of spare grid capacity. Using satellite imagery, we assess solar and wind potential near 3,890 U.S. fossil and renewable plants. By 2030, we find that existing fossil plants could host up to 597 GW of economically viable solar and wind without exceeding the existing interconnection capacity of each site. Existing renewable plants could host an additional 260 GW of firm capacity—comprising storage paired with added solar and wind capacity. These additions could accelerate clean energy deployment and enhance reliability and affordability, but realizing this potential is contingent upon regulatory reforms and coordinating the operational constraints of colocated resources.

articles.title: Neuromodulatory control of cortical function: Cell-type-specific regulation of neuronal information transfer
articles.titleEn: Neuromodulatory control of cortical function: Cell-type-specific regulation of neuronal information transfer
articles.abstract: Neuromodulatory systems such as dopamine and acetylcholine enable cortical circuits to rapidly shift between behavioral states, yet it remains unclear how receptor-specific signaling reshapes what single neurons compute. Here, we combined whole-cell recordings from excitatory and inhibitory neurons in layer 2/3 of mouse somatosensory cortex with information-theoretic analyses under frozen-noise stimulation. We quantified stimulus-to-spike information transfer and profiled each neuron across four functional domains: passive membrane biophysics, action potential dynamics, intrinsic adaptation currents, and input feature selectivity captured by spike-triggered averages. Activation of D1, D2, or M1 receptors revealed three main findings. First, neuromodulators altered fractional information and firing output in a cell-type- and receptor-specific manner, demonstrating selective regulation of encoding. Second, unsupervised clustering based on functional attribute sets showed that receptor activation reorganizes baseline functional grouping, consistent with a dynamic computational phenotype. Third, multiset correlation and factor analysis revealed that neuromodulation systematically reorganizes covariance among functional domains. In excitatory neurons, dopaminergic activation decreased coordination between input feature selectivity and other functional properties while strengthening coordination among response-based features such as spike dynamics and adaptation. Inhibitory neurons, by contrast, generally exhibited increased coordination across domains. In unison, these findings identify neuromodulation as a reconfiguration signal that reshapes not only individual cellular properties, but also the statistical architecture linking them across the recorded cohort, thereby revealing a higher-dimensional mode of single-neuron regulatory control in the cortex.

articles.title: Impact of Junction Angle on Density‐Driven Secondary Flow and Mixing Rates at River Confluences: A Numerical Investigation
articles.titleEn: Impact of Junction Angle on Density‐Driven Secondary Flow and Mixing Rates at River Confluences: A Numerical Investigation
articles.abstract: It is now well understood that a small difference in the density of two rivers can cause density‐driven streamwise vortices (SOVs) to form and their mixing interface to tilt downstream of their confluence. However, much less knowledge exists pertaining to how these processes are affected by other key confluence parameters such as the discharge ratio and junction angle. This study uses eddy‐resolving simulations of an experimental confluence flume to parametrically investigate how increasing junction angle under a range of and discharge ratios affect flow structure. The findings demonstrate that increasing junction angle increases the width of the mixing interface near the apex as well as mixing rates. However, the contribution of junction angle is shown to be incidental compared to that of . Increasing has an overwhelming effect on the lateral expansion of the mixing interface, the magnitude of streamwise circulation, and ultimately, mixing rates compared to the junction angle. Increasing also increases the tilting of the mixing interface, leading to increased lateral stretching of the vertically oriented Kelvin‐Helmholtz vortices, resulting in a rapid loss in their coherence downstream. The simulations indicate the SOVs decay in the streamwise direction due to interaction with the free surface and the bed. Our use of smooth downstream corners, similar to those present at natural river confluences, suggests that the role of the junction angle has likely been overestimated in previous laboratory and modeling studies, which focused on asymmetrical junctions featuring a sharp downstream corner and a wide separation zone.

articles.title: Basin-scale evaluation of the Noah-MP land surface model for runoff and snow generation in the Missouri River Basin: insights and recommendations for parameterization scheme selection
articles.titleEn: Basin-scale evaluation of the Noah-MP land surface model for runoff and snow generation in the Missouri River Basin: insights and recommendations for parameterization scheme selection
articles.abstract: Process-based land surface models, such as the Noah-Multiparameterization (Noah-MP) model, are widely used for large-scale hydrologic simulations because of their flexibility in selecting multiple parameterization schemes. However, limited guidance on choosing appropriate configurations constrains their reliability in representing runoff and snowmelt dynamics across diverse land-cover and snow conditions. This study evaluates the default and four alternative parameterization schemes in the Noah-MP land surface model, including Runoff and Groundwater (RUN), Surface Exchange Coefficient for Heat (SFC), Frozen Soil Permeability (INF), and Snow/Soil Temperature Time Scheme (STC), across 50 Hydro-Climate Data Networks (HCDNs) in the Missouri River Basin. Model performance was evaluated using USGS streamflow observations and snow water equivalent (SWE) estimates from the University of Arizona dataset for 2014–2023. Results showed that the alternative schemes improved runoff simulation compared to the default scheme through different approaches representing key hydrological and thermodynamic processes. Specifically, the RUN, SFC, INF, and STC experiments improved the Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) by 0.19, 0.38, 0.44, and 0.14, respectively in representative subbasins, through enhanced groundwater dynamics, reduced evapotranspiration bias, improved rapid runoff response, and more accurate SWE evolution. SWE evaluation further indicates that the STC experiment most effectively reduced SWE bias in snow-dominated subbasins, though improvements in SWE did not universally translate into better runoff simulation. These results highlight the importance of basin-specific parameterization schemes within Noah-MP to improve hydrological prediction and water management across diverse hydroclimatic regions. The findings further indicate optimal parameterization schemes for different climates, land cover, and snow regimes.

articles.title: Improving photosynthate allocation dynamic simulations of crops under water stress conditions
articles.titleEn: Improving photosynthate allocation dynamic simulations of crops under water stress conditions
articles.abstract: Accurately simulating crop photosynthate allocation under water stress is critical for predicting both food security and ecosystem carbon inputs. Current crop models often rely on static or growth-stage-fixed allocation coefficients, which limits their ability to capture the physiological plasticity of crops responding to fluctuating environmental conditions. This study develops a water-driven, stage-dependent carbon allocation scheme within the Agro-C model to better represent crop responses to soil moisture variability. The scheme dynamically adjusts photosynthate allocation coefficients for roots (PR) and leaves (PL), integrates the yellow-to-green leaf ratio (YGR), and incorporates a water stress-induced leaf senescence module. By coupling carbon allocation to both soil moisture and crop development, the approach improves the representation of physiologically regulated allocation processes and enhances the realism of crop simulations. Model evaluation using extensive observation datasets for maize and wheat demonstrates substantial improvements in simulation accuracy, with R 2 values reaching 0.77–0.95 for aboveground biomass (AGB) and 0.62–0.83 for belowground biomass (BGB). These results underscore the importance of dynamically representing carbon allocation under water stress and offer an improved framework for simulating carbon–water interactions in agroecosystems.

articles.title: Development and validation of ARMS-gb v2.0: extending fast radiative transfer modeling capability to all-sky conditions for ground-based microwave radiometer retrievals
articles.titleEn: Development and validation of ARMS-gb v2.0: extending fast radiative transfer modeling capability to all-sky conditions for ground-based microwave radiometer retrievals
articles.abstract: Ground-based microwave radiometers provide continuous, all-weather observations of boundary-layer temperature and humidity, closing a critical near-surface observation gap. The Advanced Radiative Transfer Modeling System – ground-based (ARMS-gb) is a fast radiative transfer model specifically designed to simulate the brightness temperatures observed by these instruments. This paper presents ARMS-gb v2.0, which introduces a hydrometeor absorption and scattering module and an accelerated discrete ordinate method (ADOM) solver for multiple scattering. The model now simulates cloud water, rain, ice, snow, and graupel using optical-property look-up tables computed with Mie theory and the discrete dipole approximation (DDA). The existing tangent-linear and adjoint (TL/AD) modules are also extended to include hydrometeor processes, supporting all-sky retrieval and variational data assimilation. Validation against field measurements from 14- and 22-channel ground-based microwave radiometers indicates that ARMS-gb v2.0 effectively simulates brightness temperatures under cloudy non-precipitating conditions, with the mean observed minus simulated brightness temperature generally within 1 K of the corresponding clear-sky baseline. Compared with ARMS-gb v1.0, which neglects cloud effects, the root mean square error (RMSE) under cloudy conditions decreases by 1–2 K in the water-vapor band, most notably at 30 GHz, where the coefficient of determination ( R 2 ) increases from 0.55 to 0.77. In the weak oxygen band, where frozen hydrometeors have stronger scattering effects, the observation-minus-background (O–B) decreases by 3–4 K. At 51 GHz, the RMSE decreases from 5.23 to 3.22 K, and R 2 increases from 0.52 to 0.81. Moreover, the results indicate that the DDA model slightly outperforms the Mie model in characterizing frozen hydrometeors at these channels. However, large O–B departures remain during precipitation events, with RMSE values in the water-vapor absorption band reaching 30–40 K, reflecting rain-contaminated measurement effects and atmospheric hydrometeor uncertainties that require dedicated quality control and observation-error modeling before assimilation or retrieval applications.

articles.title: High-resolution global groundwater storage anomalies: a 1 km downscaled dataset
articles.titleEn: High-resolution global groundwater storage anomalies: a 1 km downscaled dataset
articles.abstract: Groundwater depletion poses a challenge to water security, but the coarse spatial resolution of Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment (GRACE) observations limits the characterization of groundwater variability at regional and local scales. Here, we present a 1 km monthly global groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) dataset covering April 2002–December 2020. The dataset was generated using Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) for temporal gap filling, 19 high-resolution hydroclimatic and geophysical predictors, and aquifer-stratified machine-learning downscaling. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and deep neural networks (DNN) were evaluated as candidate models, and XGBoost was selected for dataset production based on internal, cross-scale, and in-situ evaluations. When aggregated to the original GRACE scale, the 1 km product agreed closely with the original GWSA ( R 2 = 0.972, RMSE = 2.10 cm). Independent evaluation used a global archive of 152 069 groundwater-monitoring wells and a 1° spatial-block calibration–validation design. Effective specific yield ( S yeff ) was estimated from calibration blocks and transferred to held-out blocks before comparison at a common 0.25° grid. For XGBoost, the held-out evaluation yielded R 2 = 0.538, RMSE = 0.378 cm yr −1 , and Bias = 0.106 cm yr −1 . The association between modeled and observation-derived trends remained similar under ± 30 % perturbations in S yeff , although amplitude-related metrics were more sensitive to the conversion coefficient. Standardized time-series comparisons and monthly evaluations of representative aquifers showed better agreement for long-term variability than for seasonal variability. Comparisons with published regional estimates showed close agreement in the North China Plain, weaker depletion magnitudes in northwestern India and California, and a trend-sign mismatch in the High Plains Aquifer during 2003–2013. Experiments using CSR, JPL, H08, and WaterGAP also showed that reconstruction performance and predictor importance depend on the target product. The dataset provides kilometre-scale estimates of groundwater-storage variability under the large-scale GRACE constraint. Local interpretation of the reconstructed spatial patterns requires additional groundwater-level, abstraction, and hydrogeological observations. The 1 km monthly global GWSA dataset is openly available from the National Cryosphere Desert Data Center at https://doi.org/10.12072/ncdc.hydrology.db7323.2026 (Fan et al., 2026).

articles.title: TED: a global temperature-driven thermoelastic displacement dataset for GNSS reference stations (2000–2023)
articles.titleEn: TED: a global temperature-driven thermoelastic displacement dataset for GNSS reference stations (2000–2023)
articles.abstract: Nonlinear variations in GNSS station height time series include contributions from non-tidal mass loading and temperature-driven thermoelastic displacement (TED). However, a globally consistent station-level TED product has not been widely available. Here we present a global dataset of vertical TED for approximately 14 000 GNSS stations over 2000–2023, generated using a full-spectrum layered finite-element model. The model is driven by hourly ERA5 soil-temperature forcing and parameterized with SoilGrids-derived depth-dependent subsurface properties, allowing within-day temperature variability to be incorporated into daily TED time series that retain seasonal and nonseasonal components. For the 2612 stations with documented foundation-depth information, site-information-constrained solutions agree closely with SoilGrids-based solutions, with annual-amplitude differences mostly about 0.01–0.03 mm and annual-phase differences generally within 1–3°. Sensitivity tests using ± 10 % perturbations in the linear thermal expansion coefficient, thermal diffusivity, and Young's modulus indicate that the amplitude and phase of the annual TED component are stable under reasonable parameter uncertainty. Globally, annual TED amplitudes are mostly within about 0.2–1.2 mm and locally exceed 1.5 mm, with larger signals concentrated in arid inland and continental regions. The percentile-based peak-to-peak variability of the full daily TED series commonly reaches 2–4 mm and locally approaches 5–6 mm. When applied alone to GNSS height time series, TED produces positive WRMS reductions at about 79 % of the assessed stations, with most improvements within 3 %–5 % and the largest reductions reaching about 10 %. The dataset is publicly available for direct use in GNSS height time series correction and related geophysical applications: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21069958 (Lu et al., 2026a).

articles.title: Linking sea–air and benthic methane fluxes across seasons in a tropical seagrass meadow of Taiwan
articles.titleEn: Linking sea–air and benthic methane fluxes across seasons in a tropical seagrass meadow of Taiwan
articles.abstract: Seagrass meadows are important blue carbon ecosystems that sequester large amounts of organic carbon but can also emit methane (CH 4 ), potentially offsetting part of their climate mitigation benefits. However, the seasonal and diurnal dynamics of CH 4 production and emissions in tropical seagrass ecosystems remain poorly understood. This study presents the first integrated assessment of CH 4 cycling in the Haikou seagrass meadow, southern Taiwan. Field campaigns conducted between May 2022 and June 2023 combined surface water sampling, in situ benthic chamber incubations, and porewater profiling in a Thalassia hemprichii–Halophila pinifolia seagrass meadow to quantify CH 4 dynamics at both the sediment-to-water and sea-to-air interfaces. The seagrass meadow exhibited higher dissolved CH 4 concentrations and sea-to-air CH 4 fluxes than adjacent coastal waters, confirming that it functions as a localized atmospheric CH 4 hotspot. Nighttime dissolved CH 4 concentrations generally exceeded daytime values, reflecting diurnal variations in oxygen availability, whereas seasonal variability in sea-to-air CH 4 fluxes was primarily driven by wind speed. Mean sediment-to-water and sea-to-air CH 4 fluxes were 88.2±41.2 and 4.9±2.2µmol m −2 d −1 , respectively. Despite substantial benthic CH 4 production, atmospheric emissions remained comparatively low, indicating a marked decoupling between sediment-to-water and sea-to-air CH 4 fluxes. This decoupling suggests that much of the sediment-derived CH 4 was transported laterally by tidal exchange and coastal circulation before atmospheric release, with microbial oxidation acting as an additional sink. Compared with adjacent bare sand sediments, seagrass sediments maintained higher baseline CH 4 production rates and benthic fluxes owing to greater organic matter availability and favorable microbial conditions, whereas unvegetated sandy sediments generally exhibited low CH 4 production but produced episodic CH 4 pulses following storm-induced sediment disturbance. Elevated porewater CH 4 concentrations during summer and autumn further indicated enhanced methanogenesis associated with organic matter accumulation under calmer hydrodynamic conditions. Overall, these findings demonstrate that CH 4 cycling in tropical seagrass meadows is jointly regulated by biological processes and hydrodynamic conditions, highlighting the need to consider both CH 4 emissions and carbon sequestration when evaluating the climate benefits of blue carbon ecosystems.

articles.title: Detecting long-term canopy change and vegetation shifts in northern peatlands using LAI and climate data
articles.titleEn: Detecting long-term canopy change and vegetation shifts in northern peatlands using LAI and climate data
articles.abstract: Northern peatlands store vast amounts of carbon, part of which might be released to the atmosphere as climate warming alters peatland canopies. To track these changes, we analysed recent greening and browning across northern peatlands, defined here as increases and decreases in leaf area index (LAI), from 2001 to 2023. We assessed vegetation change using gap-filled, sensor-independent LAI climate data record at 500 m resolution across the peatland-dominated pixels north of 45° N, defined as pixels with at least 90 % mapped peatland cover and no detected wildfire during 2001–2023. To our knowledge, our results provide the first multi-decadal assessment of peatland canopy change based strictly on mapped peatlands rather than on the broader Arctic and boreal domain in which peatlands are usually embedded. Although greening was widespread at the pixel level (77 % of studied peatlands; greening-to-browning ratio 3.5:1), the area-weighted LAI trend at the map scale was not significant. LAI anomalies were weakly positively correlated with air temperature and weakly negatively correlated with precipitation; multi-year mean annual precipitation, rather than air temperature, was retained in the model of long-term LAI trends. Higher tree cover was associated with less greening, but this association was weaker in peatlands with deciduous needleleaf cover and where precipitation was higher. Most peatland pixels showed a linear LAI trend with no breakpoints; where non-linear trends occurred, their breakpoints were often temporally aligned with phase shifts in the Pacific Decadal Oscillation. These non-linear trends differed by region: trends in which LAI first decreased and then increased were concentrated in West Siberia, whereas trends in which LAI first increased and then decreased were widespread across Europe, northeastern Asia, and Canada. Protected peatlands did not show different LAI trends once differences in climate and canopy were accounted for. Overall, recent peatland canopy change was not a uniform increase in greenness but rather reflected moisture-sensitive, tree-composition-dependent responses modulated by decadal climate variability.

articles.title: Application of radar remote sensing for cyclone damage mapping in Bangladesh: a coherence-based approach
articles.titleEn: Application of radar remote sensing for cyclone damage mapping in Bangladesh: a coherence-based approach
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Rapid and reliable assessment of cyclone-induced damage remains a major challenge in coastal regions where cloud cover and limited accessibility constrain conventional approaches. This study presents a coherence-based Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) framework for identifying and quantifying cyclone-induced surface changes in the coastal districts of Bangladesh. Multi-temporal Sentinel-1 data were analyzed using interferometric coherence to capture spatial and temporal variations associated with five major cyclones: Amphan (2020), Sitrang (2022), Mocha (2023), Hamoon (2023), and Remal (2024). A time-series approach incorporating multiple pre-, during-, and post-event image pairs was implemented to distinguish cyclone-driven changes from natural surface variability and to improve detection reliability. The results reveal a consistent decline in coherence during cyclone events, followed by gradual recovery. Spatial analysis indicates that areas of significant coherence loss correspond to zones affected by flooding, vegetation damage, and structural disruption. Estimated damage extents varied across cyclones, with Remal (2024) showing the largest affected area (∼ 601 km 2 ), followed by Mocha (∼ 474 km 2 ), Amphan (∼ 288 km 2 ), Sitrang (∼ 122 km 2 ), and Hamoon (∼ 117 km 2 ). Validation using field observations and secondary data yielded an overall classification accuracy of 94 %, confirming the robustness of the coherence-based approach. Complementary inundation mapping further demonstrated that coherence captures a broader spectrum of cyclone impacts beyond flood extent alone, including wind-induced damage and geomorphic changes. This study establishes multi-temporal SAR coherence analysis as a scalable, cloud-independent, and operationally effective tool for rapid post-cyclone damage assessment. The proposed framework enhances the reliability of disaster monitoring in complex coastal environments and offers strong potential for integration into near-real-time disaster response systems. Future research should focus on integrating multi-sensor datasets and long-term coherence time series to refine damage characterization and reduce uncertainty.

articles.title: Closed-loop photoreactor design enabled by machine learning and digital twins
articles.titleEn: Closed-loop photoreactor design enabled by machine learning and digital twins
articles.abstract: Designing efficient photoreactors remains challenging due to the complex interplay of reflection, scattering, and absorption. Here, we introduce a closed-loop workflow integrating ray-tracing digital twins with multi-objective Bayesian optimization to design photoreactors with high photon capture and uniform irradiation. A digital 3D reactor model is calibrated using measured emission characteristics, reflectivity data, and geometrical properties and validated against potassium ferrioxalate actinometry. The validated model explores reflector shape and vial positioning, identifying geometries that maximize incident photon flux while maintaining homogeneity across 16 vials. Experimental validation using a photocatalytic Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling shows that reaction yields track simulated photon flux. The optimized reactor is further applied to quantum-yield screening, enabling mechanistic insights across diverse conditions in a single experiment. This work establishes an experimentally validated virtual co-design framework in which machine learning and digital twins accelerate photoreactor development and support quantitative understanding of photochemical processes.

articles.title: Nuclear adaptation to intracellular mechanical forces regulates the phagocytic capacity of Drosophila macrophages in vivo
articles.titleEn: Nuclear adaptation to intracellular mechanical forces regulates the phagocytic capacity of Drosophila macrophages in vivo
articles.abstract: How macrophages fine-tune their appetite to fulfil their clearance role is incompletely understood. Phagocytosis exacerbates cytoplasmic crowding, but whether macrophages can sense this increase and use it to regulate their phagocytic capacity has never been investigated. Here, we test the hypothesis that phagosomes exert a strain on the nucleus, which in turn responds to the intracellular mechanical inputs influencing macrophage appetite. Combining genetic manipulation and live in vivo imaging, we show that engulfed apoptotic bodies indent and deform the nucleus of Drosophila embryonic macrophages, and that phagocytosis increases Lamin B levels. Importantly, we show that silencing Lamin B or components of the LINC complex negatively regulates apoptotic body engulfment in vivo. Thus, we demonstrate that phagosome-induced nuclear molecular and mechanical adaptations are critical for Drosophila embryonic macrophages to sustain apoptotic corpse uptake, thereby unveiling a role for nuclear plasticity in the regulation of macrophage phagocytic capacity in vivo.

articles.title: The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
articles.titleEn: The 2023 North Atlantic marine heatwave could have evolved into a far more extreme event
articles.abstract: In 2023, the North Atlantic Ocean experienced a marine heatwave of unprecedented intensity and duration, raising the question of whether substantially more severe outcomes were physically plausible under comparable present-day preconditioning, and which processes could produce them. Here, we apply ensemble boosting to a coupled Earth system model to generate physically consistent alternative evolutions of a 2023-like event. The boosted ensemble produced marine heatwaves lasting up to 579 days, reaching maximum intensities of 4.5 °C above climatology and cumulative intensities of 717 °C·days, compared with 240 days, 2.9 °C and 224 °C·days in observations. Detailed analyses of the longest and most intense events highlight contrasting roles for persistent Euro-Atlantic high pressure, reduced turbulent heat loss, enhanced shortwave radiation and upper-ocean heat redistribution. Finally, we place these present-day storylines in the context of future warming, showing that events comparable to the observed 2023 event become increasingly common as global warming progresses.

articles.title: Transforming electrified railway into mechanical energy storage for electricity system decarbonization
articles.titleEn: Transforming electrified railway into mechanical energy storage for electricity system decarbonization
articles.abstract: Decarbonizing electricity requires vast energy storage capacity worldwide, but constructing dedicated storage assets creates substantial capital, material and embodied carbon burdens. Electrified railways already exchange energy with electricity systems through traction and regenerative braking, but their inherent potential as mechanical energy storage remains unexploited. Here we show that modulation of train operations can transform electrified railways into Electrified Rail-Based Energy Storage. By analyzing 326,034 inter-stop train operations, we estimate its global potential at 190 gigawatts in 2025 and 315–579 gigawatts by 2050. Capacity expansion models for China, Europe and India indicate that it can reduce investment in conventional storage by 11.9–20.0%, corresponding to an extrapolated global value of US$14.9–35.1 billion annually. Without increasing total system cost, electricity systems with this flexible resource could further reduce operational CO 2 emissions by 94.3–258.9 million tonnes per year. Electrified railways can therefore complement conventional storage technologies for electricity system decarbonization.

articles.title: Resolving short-term meteorological variability amplifies projected glacier loss and sea-level rise
articles.titleEn: Resolving short-term meteorological variability amplifies projected glacier loss and sea-level rise
articles.abstract: Global glacier models typically rely on temperature-index mass balance calculations forced with aggregated meteorological data, limiting their ability to resolve short-term variability. Here, we develop a daily-resolution version of the Global Glacier Evolution Model (GloGEM), which we apply globally and compare against the monthly configuration. Our results show that the daily model more closely reproduces mass balance observations and provides a more detailed representation of glacier runoff. Resolving high-frequency forcing, or accounting for its effects through parameterisations, is therefore essential for robust glacier projections, while its omission may systematically underestimate future glacier loss.

articles.title: Controlling the shell growth mechanism and interfacial oxidation of InAs/ZnSe quantum dots for shortwave infrared emission
articles.titleEn: Controlling the shell growth mechanism and interfacial oxidation of InAs/ZnSe quantum dots for shortwave infrared emission
articles.abstract: Short-wave infrared (SWIR) emitters underpin applications in communication, imaging and sensing, yet efficient, scalable devices remain limited. However, developing heavy-metal-free InAs CQDs for emission beyond 1400 nm is hindered by lattice mismatch during core/shell growth, which degrades photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY). Furthermore, integrating CQDs into LEDs often introduces severe interfacial quenching and intrinsic charge imbalances. Here we report a highly efficient heavy-metal-free SWIR LED operating at 1525 nm, enabled by tailored injection strategies and oxidation-induced interfacial engineering. Optimized high-temperature ZnCl₂ treatment and continuous precursor injection improve shell nucleation and growth, while controlled interfacial oxidation is associated with reduced shell-thickness-dependent strain signatures and improved PLQY retention during shell thickening. Together, these strategies yield measured PLQYs exceeding 55% for emission beyond 1400 nm. Moreover, we demonstrate that incorporating a semiconducting InAs CQD interlayer effectively suppresses interfacial quenching and regulates electron over-injection. Combined with a doped hole-transport layer to reduce series resistance, our optimized devices achieve a maximum external quantum efficiency of 3.5% and a record radiance of ~17 W sr −1 m −2 , alongside a T50 operational lifetime of 16 h. Our findings suggest that integrating mechanism-driven shell growth with rational device engineering offers a strategy to overcome current bottlenecks in colloidal emitters, facilitating the transition toward short-wave infrared applications.

articles.title: Short-term effectiveness and impact of Vaxchora vaccine during the 2024 cholera outbreak in Mayotte
articles.titleEn: Short-term effectiveness and impact of Vaxchora vaccine during the 2024 cholera outbreak in Mayotte
articles.abstract: Global cholera resurgence and vaccine shortage have driven the adoption of reactive one-dose strategies with killed oral cholera vaccines (OCVs). The live-attenuated vaccine CVD 103-HgR (Vaxchora) shows high efficacy in human challenge studies, but its real-world effectiveness in outbreaks is unknown. Here, we analyze the 2024 outbreak in Mayotte, focusing on Koungou village, which had high cholera incidence and vaccine uptake. We develop several stochastic models and calibrate them to daily cases by vaccination status. In total, 3354 individuals (71%) of Koungou’s at-risk population ( n = 4733) received CVD 103-HgR, and 77 cases were confirmed, with symptom onset between 19 April and 7 July 2024. At baseline, we estimate a basic reproduction number $${R}_{0}$$ R 0 of 1.5 (95% credible interval (CrI): 1.2, 1.9) and a CVD 103-HgR effectiveness in preventing cholera of 87% (95% CrI: 74, 99), remaining between 75% and 91% across scenarios. Counterfactual simulations estimate 536 (95% CrI: 240, 824) cases averted at baseline, with a range of point estimates from 152 to 1228 across sensitivity analyses. Rapid single-dose CVD 103-HgR deployment is associated with high effectiveness during a real‑world outbreak, with a substantial but more uncertain population impact, supporting the inclusion of live-attenuated OCVs in reactive strategies when necessary.

articles.title: Projected intensification of soil salinization in global drylands under future aridity increase
articles.titleEn: Projected intensification of soil salinization in global drylands under future aridity increase
articles.abstract: Soil salinization threatens agricultural production, water management, and ecosystem health. Yet, how increasing aridity will reshape 21st-century soil salinity patterns across drylands, particularly in croplands, remains unclear. Here, we compile a relatively comprehensive global soil salinity dataset from the past two decades, projecting future dryland soil salinity dynamics using climate-driven machine learning models with multiple covariates, including dynamic dryland extent and human influences. Our results show an 8% expansion of global drylands saline soils under increasing aridity by 2100 (SSP5-8.5) relative to 2004–2023. Southwestern US, Mexico, southern Europe, central South America, eastern and southern Africa are highest-risk hotspots. We further show dryland croplands face serious salinization, especially irrigated systems, where half of these newly salinized areas project more than 4.9% (maize), 17.2% (dryland rice), 3.3% (sorghum), and 21.2% (wheat) potential production losses. Our findings inform long-term adaptation strategies to mitigate emerging salinization risks and sustain water and food security.

articles.title: Intensifying Tropical Cyclones and Expanding Renewable Energy Call for Climate‐Resilient Planning in China
articles.titleEn: Intensifying Tropical Cyclones and Expanding Renewable Energy Call for Climate‐Resilient Planning in China
articles.abstract: Variable renewable energy (VRE) is central to power system decarbonization for climate mitigation, yet its rapid expansion places growing VRE infrastructure at risk from tropical cyclones (TCs). With TCs projected to intensify, such risks remain poorly quantified at policy‐relevant scales, potentially exposing power systems to unforeseen disruption and damage. Here, we develop a spatially resolved risk projection model by coupling a physics‐based TC hazard module with a power system optimization module to assess the impact of TC climatology change on VRE expansion in China. We find that the TC‐induced economic losses to VRE are projected to increase 10‐ to 20‐fold relative to a historical baseline (1975–2014) of 0.37 billion USD yr −1 by the late 21st century (2061–2100), with wind power accounting for 87%–91% of this increase. The decomposition analysis shows that exposure dominates (contributing 44%–49%) the increase in economic loss growth over 2021–2060, whereas hazard‐exposure interaction dominates (contributing 49%–67%) over 2061–2100. We further identify the optimal strengthening metric, which can offset 54%–67% of the projected economic losses. This framework shifts disaster‐risk assessment from reactive recovery to proactive infrastructure resilience planning, providing a scalable template for climate‐resilient coastal energy transitions worldwide.

articles.title: Policy‐Driven Evolution of Sediment in the Yellow River Basin over the Past 2000 Years
articles.titleEn: Policy‐Driven Evolution of Sediment in the Yellow River Basin over the Past 2000 Years
articles.abstract: River sediment load serves as a typical indicator of the interaction between human activities and the natural environment, and historical policies have profoundly altered basin sediment transport processes. In this study, we constructed a quantitative analytical framework based on the policy index to systematically trace the evolutionary trajectories of ecological conservation, land use, and taxation policies in the Yellow River Basin over the past two millennia. We reveal how policy‐driven human activities have reshaped land use patterns, and how these changes are linked to the long‐term response mechanism of sediment load from the Yellow River. We find that prior to the 1970s, development‐oriented policies promoted cropland expansion via tax incentives and land allocation, leading to vegetation destruction and intensified soil erosion, and sediment load fluctuated and rose to exceed 1.3 Gt/yr. After the 1970s, conservation‐oriented policies restricted development and implemented systematic restoration, causing sediment load to decline to 0.24 Gt/yr in 2020. Human activities contributed 70.56% and 75% of sediment load variation in these two stages, respectively, playing a dominant role, while climate change accounted for less than 30% of the variation in both periods, acting as a periodic regulatory factor. These mechanisms ultimately form the cascading effect of “policies → human activities → land use → sediment load.” The “policy‐response” linkage established in this study provides a quantitative paradigm for understanding millennial‐scale human‐water relationships, and demonstrates the decisive role of policies in river basin governance.

articles.title: The Alarming Trend of Water Weaponization During the Russian War in Ukraine
articles.titleEn: The Alarming Trend of Water Weaponization During the Russian War in Ukraine
articles.abstract: Water plays a critical role in sustaining civilian populations during armed conflict, yet its deliberate disruption is increasingly reported in contemporary warfare. Despite growing attention to the topic of water weaponization, the concept remains inconsistently defined throughout humanitarian, environmental, and legal literature. This study examines existing conceptualizations of water weaponization and combines them into a broader analytical framework that considers any actions that impair the availability, quality, or accessibility of water for civilian populations as weaponization of water. Using this framework, the study analyzes documented cases from the Russian war in Ukraine and evaluates the limitations of existing international legal mechanisms intended to protect water during armed conflict. The discussion is built on a combination of a scoping literature review and semi‐structured expert interviews. The findings demonstrate that water weaponization extends beyond direct attacks on hydraulic infrastructure and water supply systems, or conflict‐related water pollution. Instead, many consequences arise through indirect impacts and interconnected infrastructure systems. Disruptions to energy, industrial, and water sectors amplify humanitarian and environmental risks that exceed their immediate military significance. The study also reveals persistent challenges in evidence collection, attribution of responsibility, environmental monitoring, and enforcement of existing international legal protections in active conflict settings. By linking empirical evidence from Ukraine with broader debates on water security and conflict, the study contributes to ongoing efforts to clarify the scope of water weaponization and calls for the need to strengthen approaches for assessing water‐related harms during warfare.

articles.title: Improving AquaCrop Root‐Zone Soil Moisture by Assimilating SMAP Surface Soil Moisture
articles.titleEn: Improving AquaCrop Root‐Zone Soil Moisture by Assimilating SMAP Surface Soil Moisture
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Root‐zone soil moisture (RZSM) strongly controls crop development in process‐based crop models, yet most satellite missions observe only near‐surface moisture. We propose a framework to assimilate soil moisture active passive (SMAP) Level‐2 surface soil moisture retrievals into AquaCrop to improve RZSM over European croplands (0.1° resolution, 2015–2023). We assimilate either these SMAP retrievals directly, or exponentially filtered SMAP retrievals optimized for specific target depths (0–30, 0–60, and 0–100 cm), always bias‐corrected using seasonally varying cumulative distribution function matching within an ensemble Kalman filter. AquaCrop's cascading, threshold‐based soil water balance exhibits much weaker short‐term vertical coupling than in situ observations, limiting the downward propagation of surface‐only updates. Consistent with this behavior, assimilation of both surface retrievals and exponentially filtered SMAP data improves topsoil moisture (0–30 cm), while subsoil (30–100 cm) and RZSM (0–100 cm) improve most when assimilating exponentially filtered observations that embed temporal persistence of deeper soil depths. Best overall RZSM performance is obtained by assimilating SMAP data exponentially filtered to a target depth of 0–60 cm, yielding widespread increases in anomaly correlation against in situ observations. Improvements in soil moisture translate only weakly and inconsistently to vegetation space: updated soil moisture better explains interannual variability in satellite vegetation indicators but improvements in canopy cover and biomass simulated by AquaCrop remain limited. These results indicate that while exponential‐filter‐based soil moisture assimilation robustly improves deeper moisture, joint assimilation of soil moisture and vegetation observations is needed to better constrain soil–plant coupling and ensure that soil moisture corrections propagate more effectively into crop growth predictions.

articles.title: Satellite‐Based Estimates of Irrigation Water Use Versus Modeling Reconstructions: How Much do They Differ?
articles.titleEn: Satellite‐Based Estimates of Irrigation Water Use Versus Modeling Reconstructions: How Much do They Differ?
articles.abstract: Knowing water amounts destined for agricultural practices, essentially consisting of irrigation water use (IWU), is essential for water resources management. Although explicit and consistent information on IWU is generally lacking worldwide, remote sensing and modeling platforms offer valuable solutions for estimating it. The objective of this work is to perform an intercomparison between satellite‐based IWU products and modeling reconstructions over four main irrigation hotspots worldwide: the Contiguous United States (CONUS), the Ebro basin (Spain), India, and the Murray‐Darling basin (Australia). Remote‐sensing‐based IWU estimated through Soil‐Moisture‐Inversion (SM‐Inversion) and SM‐Delta approaches are considered. As modeled data, five Global Hydrological Models are evaluated: H08, PCR‐GLOBWB, WaterGAP, LPJmL, and QUAlloc. Reference irrigation volumes are exploited to assess which source is more reliable. Over CONUS and Murray‐Darling basin, lower discrepancies between data sources (satellite or modeling) are detected. Referring to spatially‐averaged IWU magnitudes, the comparison over CONUS provides ranging from 9.52 to 12.21 mm/month, between 3.24 and 7.06 mm/month, and Pearson correlation () from 0.77 to 0.90. The same intervals for the Murray‐Darling basin are 8.04–17.70 mm/month for , 4.81–12.63 mm/month for , and 0.42–0.85 for . Consequently, over such areas, similar performances in reproducing actual irrigation amounts by satellite estimates and modeling reconstructions, when available, are found. Over the Ebro basin, where the strongest discrepancies are found, satellite‐based data sets outperform model outputs in reproducing reference data. The lack of in situ observations for India prevents a clear assessment of the results, but insights on differences introduced by parametrizations are established.

articles.title: Alaskan Glaciers in a Warming Climate
articles.titleEn: Alaskan Glaciers in a Warming Climate
articles.abstract: Glaciers across Alaska are undergoing rapid mass loss, with implications for sea‐level rise, natural hazards, water resources, and more. Here, we utilize new snowline and melt extent observations of Alaskan glaciers at high spatiotemporal resolutions to improve projections to 2100. Specifically, we incorporate these observations into the calibration scheme for the large‐scale Python Glacier Evolution Model (PyGEM), and subsequently simulate future changes under various climate scenarios. We estimate that glaciers in Alaska will lose 49 ± 17% to 73 ± 26% of their 2015 mass by the end of the century, depending on the future climate. Nearly all small glaciers ( 2 ) will disappear by 2100 regardless of the climate scenario, along with the smallest glacierized subregions of Alaska, namely, the Brooks and Talkeetna ranges. Across larger subregions, negative mass balance is projected to peak in the middle of the 21st century for the modest future warming scenario (i.e., SSP1‐2.6), while negative mass balance continues to increase to 2100 for the most aggressive future warming scenario (SSP5‐8.5). Much of these changes are attributed to increasing temperatures that cause greater melt in addition to a shift in early‐winter precipitation from snow to rain which reduces accumulation and enhances melt by exposing the underlying ice earlier in the next ablation season. Of the remaining glaciers in 2100, 15%–60%, depending on the future climate, have no accumulation area and are thus committed to disappearance. Overall, the widespread loss of glaciers in Alaska by 2100 has implications on ecology, water resources, natural hazards, and tourism across the region.

articles.title: Investigating Cloud–Radiation Error Compensations Stemming From Climate Model Calibration
articles.titleEn: Investigating Cloud–Radiation Error Compensations Stemming From Climate Model Calibration
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Compensating errors are an obstacle to the development of climate models. We wonder if systematic errors in simulated cloud properties might result from forced error compensation due to targeting top‐of‐atmosphere radiative fluxes in the tuning process while using an inaccurate radiative transfer (RT) parameterization. Here, we investigate the extent to which parametric and structural errors in state‐of‐the‐art RT models might be offset by errors relating to cloud properties, and under what circumstances. For this we run tuning experiments with a Single‐Column version of a climate Model (SCM), with and without a parameterization of 3D radiative effects of clouds, targeting reference solar fluxes calculated on Large‐Eddy Simulation cloud fields. In a first set of tuning experiments, the parameters that control cloud geometry in the radiative transfer code are tuned assuming perfect cloud profiles. Compensation mechanisms are found between cloud geometry effects, notably between cloud vertical overlap and 3D effects. In a second set of experiments, cloud geometry parameters are set to nominal values, and free parameters of the boundary layer and cloud parameterizations are tuned, still targeting radiative metrics. We found that, when 3D effects are neglected in these experiments, reasonable fluxes are obtained only at the expense of overestimated cloud fractions, partly compensating for underestimated cloud reflectivity at low sun. Targeting mean solar‐angle fluxes instead of detailed ones removes this mechanism entirely. This study both enlightens some compensation errors specific to cloud–radiation interaction and illustrates more generally how the tuning tool can be used to study and quantify compensating errors.

articles.title: Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals
articles.titleEn: Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals
articles.abstract: Coral bleaching, the temperature-induced loss of dinoflagellate symbionts, is a major driver of global coral reef decline. Although corals can regain symbionts through repopulation of residual symbionts or via environmental acquisition, these processes are often too slow to prevent coral mortality. Mechanisms that enable rapid and effective symbiont reintroduction leading to full recovery remain largely unknown. Here, we demonstrate coral bleaching recovery through contact-mediated transfer of symbionts from healthy corals using small coral fragments. We show that symbiont transfer is rapid, occurring over days to weeks, and highly efficient, with only brief physical contact with healthy corals required. A single week of contact, and in some cases as few as 3 days, provides sufficient symbionts to initiate sustained and full self-recovery. By 1 week, symbiont population doubling time is approximately 4 days, up to an order of magnitude faster than most recovery times for corals in the field. We identify tissue fusion as the mechanism enabling directional symbiont transfer from healthy to bleached coral tissue. As a result, contact-dependent recovery is restricted to corals of the same genet, whereas heterologous genet pairings trigger antagonistic interactions. However, symbiont transfer via polyp uptake occurs immediately upon contact in both same-genet and mixed-genet pairings, revealing an additional, slower pathway for symbiont transfer that is insufficient on its own to support colony recovery. Collectively, these findings reveal a previously unrecognized natural process for efficiently reintroducing symbionts to bleached corals, providing a foundation for research into potential recovery interventions.

articles.title: Climate choices and attention are shaped more by politics than weather
articles.titleEn: Climate choices and attention are shaped more by politics than weather

articles.title: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure
articles.titleEn: Political affiliation impacts climate attention and choice beyond extreme weather exposure
articles.abstract: Political polarization and increasing exposure to extreme weather can shape public engagement with climate change, yet the underlying psychological mechanisms remain unclear. In this Registered Report, we examine how political affiliation, extreme weather exposure and subjective attribution influence climate-relevant information search and decision-making in a US sample ( N = 1,451). We combined a process-tracing paradigm within an incentivized decision task involving real carbon emissions with objective data on extreme weather exposure. Democrats attended more to carbon emission information and made more pro-climate choices than Republicans, with no evidence of moderation by objective extreme weather exposure. The subjective attribution of extreme weather to climate change was associated with greater attention to carbon information, more pro-climate choices and moderated the effects of exposure on both outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of political affiliation in climate-relevant decision-making and suggest that extreme weather effects depend less on exposure itself than on how these experiences are interpreted.

articles.title: Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections
articles.titleEn: Palaeoclimate constraints narrow uncertainty in future Arctic winter sea ice projections
articles.abstract: Arctic sea ice decline has been observed across all seasons and is projected to continue in the future. Relative to historical observations, climate models show their largest biases and uncertainties during winter, when ice cover strongly regulates air–sea heat exchange, ocean mixing and atmospheric circulation. Palaeoclimate records offer opportunities to evaluate model performance beyond the historical period, but applications have remained largely qualitative. Here we compile an Arctic-wide database of mid-Holocene (5–7 thousand years ago) biomarkers to assess sea ice simulations of this past warm period. Using a recently developed proxy system model, we present a Bayesian palaeoclimate model weighting scheme that refines the multi-model mean winter sea ice extent through fully quantitative proxy-model comparisons, accounting for model interdependence and non-stationary proxy seasonality. We demonstrate that, by adjusting the contribution of each model to the ensemble mean based on proxy evidence, model weights can eliminate biases and reduce uncertainties by 85%, to the level of interannual variability. Weighted projections using the same climate models indicate that future winter sea ice extent may be nearly 1 million km 2 lower than prior estimates across forthcoming decades and possible emissions scenarios, with broad implications for Arctic ecosystems, mid-latitude weather, and cryosphere stability.

articles.title: Big Data for Small Streams: Leveraging a Coarse National Model to Enhance Fine‐Resolution Stream Temperature Predictions
articles.titleEn: Big Data for Small Streams: Leveraging a Coarse National Model to Enhance Fine‐Resolution Stream Temperature Predictions
articles.abstract: Predictive stream temperature models are commonly used to address spatial and temporal gaps in observational data because stream temperature information is essential for environmental management decisions. National models capture broad patterns driven by climate, topography, and seasonality, but often lack the spatial resolution to simulate fine‐scale variation in groundwater discharge, riparian shading, or tributary inflows. In contrast, watershed models may simulate finer‐resolution patterns but miss regional drivers or be limited by scarcity of observations. To generate watershed‐extent, fine‐resolution stream temperature predictions, we developed 18 multiscale machine‐learning models that leverage (a) a broad‐extent, coarse‐resolution stream temperature model and (b) finer‐resolution observations and predictor data. The coarse‐resolution model simulates daily stream temperature across the conterminous United States on the National Hydrologic Geospatial Fabric (13.7 km median reach length; 865,364 km total). The fine‐resolution models simulate daily stream temperature on the National Hydrography Dataset Plus version 2 (1.5 km median; 5,192,808 km total). We compared multiscale models to seven purely broad‐ (national) or watershed‐extent models, testing them in eight watersheds (436–985 km 2 ) with differing hydrologic settings and under realistic data availability scenarios. Especially when observations within a watershed were scarce, multiscale models generated more accurate predictions than national or watershed‐specific models. A recurrent graph convolution neural network pretrained on coarse predictions and fine‐tuned on watershed‐specific observations was most accurate across watersheds and data scenarios. These results highlight that leveraging both coarse, national results and watershed‐specific data can increase model accuracies, particularly when observations within a watershed are spatially or temporally limited.

articles.title: How Hydrological Structural Connectivity Controls Red Soil Erosion During Multiple‐Intermittent Rainfalls
articles.titleEn: How Hydrological Structural Connectivity Controls Red Soil Erosion During Multiple‐Intermittent Rainfalls
articles.abstract: Hydrological structural connectivity is key to regulating hillslope erosion, but its formation and interactions with runoff‐sediment dynamics during intermittent rainfall remain unclear. Through simulated intermittent rainfall (three consecutive rainfall events with a 1‐day interval between each, intensities: 30, 60, 90 mm hr −1 ) combined with overland‐flow hydraulics measurements and high‐resolution UAV photogrammetry, this study reveals how hydrological structural connectivity dynamically controls erosion. Runoff‐sediment responses showed strong intensity dependence. At 30 mm hr −1 the runoff coefficient rose continuously, whereas under higher intensities it increased and then stabilized. Soil loss rates rose steadily at low intensity, followed a “rise‐then‐fall” pattern at medium intensity, and declined at high intensity. Connectivity strengthened with rainfall progression, but its growth rate declined as intensity increased. The key structural connectivity index |RF| rose with intensity (36.71, 39.36, 41.52 under 30, 60, 90 mm hr −1 , respectively; ×10 −6 ), while its growth rate decreases significantly (18.58%, 9.96%, 1.02%), showing earlier stabilization under high intensity. |RF| exhibits significant positive correlations with surface runoff, hydrodynamic parameters, and key rill morphological parameters, indicating that connectivity influences erosion processes by regulating flow pathways and convergence efficiency. Under low rainfall intensity, erosion promotes connectivity development, whereas under high rainfall intensity, an early‐established highly connected network constrains further erosion. As rainfall intensity increased, the erosion system shifts gradually from an “erosion‐driven connectivity development” regime to a “connectivity‐controlled erosion regulation” regime. This study reveals the nonlinear responses of hillslope erosion from a connectivity perspective, offering a theoretical basis for mechanism understanding and targeted conservation strategies.

articles.title: High Frequency Storm Sampling and Analysis of Hysteretic Transport Behavior Offers Insights Into Dynamic Microplastic Activation, Flux and Depletion Within a Peri‐Urban Stream
articles.titleEn: High Frequency Storm Sampling and Analysis of Hysteretic Transport Behavior Offers Insights Into Dynamic Microplastic Activation, Flux and Depletion Within a Peri‐Urban Stream
articles.abstract: Previous research has pinpointed storm events as significant potential controls of microplastic (MP) export to the oceans. Hysteretic behavior of discharge ( Q )—concentration (c) relationships for suspended sediment (SS) and solutes has been found important in understanding the dynamic activation and transport of these substances, additionally providing better estimations of long‐term loads. Due to limited availability of high frequency event‐based MP concentration data their potential hysteretic behavior has not been studied, leaving a substantial knowledge gap regarding the fate and transport mechanisms controlling MP activation and retention within catchments. We pioneer the use of high frequency MP data collected during a storm event revealing the time variable activation of different sources and transport mechanisms within a peri‐urban catchment. Surface water samples were collected before, during and after the event and combined with discharge and turbidity data to quantify MP concentrations and fluxes. Analysis of the hysteretic behavior of the Q‐c relationship revealed a clockwise hysteresis pattern with MP concentration peaking before Q , suggesting potential MP supply limitation for the sampled event. Regression analysis indicates Q to be the primary driving force promoting MP flux, with strong correlations between Q and MP concentration in rising and falling limbs. A strong Q ‐ turbidity relationship was observed only in the rising limb, potentially indicating spatial differences in the sources of SS and MPs transported in the falling limb. Total MP flux increased by 17–217 times to that of baseflow, highlighting the significance of often‐overlooked dynamics when calculating yearly MP flux.

articles.title: Time‐Varying Operation Policies With GRU‐Based Parameterization for Adaptive Multi‐Objective Reservoir Operation Under Climate Change
articles.titleEn: Time‐Varying Operation Policies With GRU‐Based Parameterization for Adaptive Multi‐Objective Reservoir Operation Under Climate Change
articles.abstract: Designing reservoir operation policies that can adapt to non‐stationary hydroclimatic conditions is a major challenge for water resources management under climate change. This study develops an adaptive dynamic operation policy (ADOP), in which Gaussian radial basis functions (RBFs) are coupled with a gated recurrent unit (GRU)‐based parameterization module that maps meteorological information to time‐varying RBF weights. Using the reservoir system in the Qingjiang River Basin, China, as a case study, ADOP is optimized using an expanded historical hydroclimatic ensemble within an evolutionary multi‐objective direct policy search (EMODPS) framework and is evaluated under both an independent historical test period and 12 GCM‐based climate scenarios. A static operation policy (SOP) and a scenario‐specific re‐optimized ideal operation policy (IOP) are used as benchmarks. Results show that ADOP outperforms SOP under both historical training and test conditions. Under future scenarios, ADOP achieves higher hypervolume than SOP in 10 of 12 scenarios, indicating the advantage of the time‐varying parameterization in out‐of‐sample conditions. Although both historically trained policies retain a performance gap relative to the re‐optimized IOP, ADOP partially mitigates this gap. The water‐level and release trajectories for representative years further demonstrate that the advantage of ADOP is associated with improved storage–release coordination. Moreover, a diagnostic comparison supports the value of the GRU‐based module, as adding meteorological inputs to a static RBF policy does not reproduce ADOP's gains. The proposed time‐varying policy provides a practical pathway for improving the adaptability of historically trained reservoir operation policies under uncertain future hydroclimatic conditions.

articles.title: Impact of Global Warming‐Induced Sea‐Surface Salt Concentration Changes on Island Groundwater System
articles.titleEn: Impact of Global Warming‐Induced Sea‐Surface Salt Concentration Changes on Island Groundwater System
articles.abstract: Global warming is altering sea‐surface salt concentration (SSC) through intensified evaporation, shifted precipitation patterns, and accelerated melting of polar ice. Subsurface freshwater in oceanic islands is typically shaped like a thin lens due to limited land area and recharge, often the primary freshwater source for local communities and highly vulnerable to seawater intrusion (SWI). However, the effects of SSC changes on freshwater lens (FWL) and SWI extent in island aquifers remain unknown, and there is little knowledge on how hydraulic conductivity (HK), local aquifer recharge (RCH) and island width ( L ) affect these effects. To end this, this study employs a simplified two‐dimensional, variable‐density island groundwater simulation model to investigate how SSC affects FWL and SWI extent across seven distinct hydrogeological scenarios, using six quantitative indicators: relative changes in (a) average water table elevation (WTE), (b) maximum WTE, (c) FWL depth, (d) FWL thickness, (e) fresh groundwater volume, (f) aquifer salt mass. Simulation results demonstrate that rising SSC increases aquifer salt mass and elevates WTE while shrinking FWL (reducing its depth, thickness, and freshwater volume), as enhanced freshwater‐saltwater density contrasts drive more vertical flow pushing FWL upward. Island aquifers with higher HK, lower RCH, or smaller L show minimal changes in WTE and aquifer salt mass but are more sensitive to SSC changes in terms of FWL depth, thickness and fresh groundwater volume. Moreover, WTE and FWL characteristics show greater sensitivity to SSC declines than to SSC increases.
